questions.q: A Deployment has `replicas: 10`, `maxUnavailable: 1`, and `maxSurge: 1`. During a rolling update, what is the range of total Pod count Kubernetes will allow?
options: Between 0 and 20 total Pods
Exactly 10 at all times, no more, no fewer
It always spikes to 20 Pods temporarily
Between 9 and 11 total Pods
questions.explain: maxSurge: 1 allows up to 1 extra Pod above the desired 10 (11 total), while maxUnavailable: 1 allows at most 1 fewer than desired to be unready (9 ready) — so the range is 9 to 11.

questions.q: What does `kubectl rollout status deployment/checkout` do?
options: Immediately deletes the Deployment
Rolls the Deployment back to the previous version
Blocks and reports on an in-progress rollout until it finishes or stalls
Scales the Deployment to zero replicas
questions.explain: rollout status is a monitoring command that blocks until the rollout completes successfully or appears stuck, letting you catch a bad rollout quickly.

questions.q: A new checkout image starts returning errors right after a rollout. What is the fastest way to revert?
options: Delete the Deployment and recreate it from scratch
kubectl rollout undo deployment/checkout
kubectl delete pod on every affected Pod
Manually find the previous image tag and edit the YAML by hand
questions.explain: Kubernetes tracks rollout history automatically. `rollout undo` reverts to the previous revision (or a specific one with --to-revision) without needing to manually hunt down the old image tag.

questions.q: Why doesn't `kubectl rollout undo` cause a full outage, even though it's reverting a bad deploy?
options: It instantly kills all Pods and restarts them at once
Rollbacks bypass the Deployment controller entirely
It only works if the Deployment has zero replicas
The rollback itself is still a RollingUpdate in reverse, replacing Pods gradually
questions.explain: A rollback uses the same RollingUpdate mechanics as a forward rollout, swapping back to the previous ReplicaSet gradually rather than all at once.

questions.q: When would Northbridge's platform team use `kubectl rollout pause` on a Deployment?
options: To permanently stop the Deployment from ever updating again
To freeze a rollout mid-flight and inspect a few new Pods under partial real traffic before committing further
pause is not a real kubectl rollout subcommand
To immediately roll back to the previous version
questions.explain: pause freezes the rollout at its current state — already-up Pods keep running, nothing new gets scheduled — until `resume` is run, useful for manual verification mid-rollout.
